p4s0.title: Russia–United Kingdom relations
p4s0.text: The Russia–United Kingdom relations (Russian: Российско-британские отношения ) is the relationship between the Russian Federation and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and it's overseas territories.

p4s1.title: Russia–United Kingdom relations
p4s1.text: Spanning nearly five centuries, it has often switched from a state of alliance to rivalry or even war.

p4s2.title: Russia–United Kingdom relations
p4s2.text: The Russians and British were allies against Napoleon, and enemies in the Crimean War of the 1850s, and rivals in the Great Game for control of central Asia in the late 19th century.

p4s3.title: Russia–United Kingdom relations
p4s3.text: They were allies again in World Wars I and II, although relations were strained by the Russian Revolution of 1917.

p4s4.title: Russia–United Kingdom relations
p4s4.text: They were at sword's point during the Cold War (1947–91).

p4s5.title: Russia–United Kingdom relations
p4s5.text: Russian big businesses had strong connections with the City of London and British corporations during the late 1990s and 2000s.

p6s0.title: Nicholas II of Russia
p6s0.text: Nicholas II or Nikolai II (Russian: Николай II Алекса́ндрович , "Nikolay II Aleksandrovich" ; 18 May [O.S. 6 May] 1868 – 17 July 1918) was the last Emperor of Russia, ruling from 1 November 1894 until his forced abdication on 15 March 1917.

p6s1.title: Nicholas II of Russia
p6s1.text: His reign saw the fall of the Russian Empire from being one of the foremost great powers of the world to economic and military collapse.

p6s2.title: Nicholas II of Russia
p6s2.text: Due to the Khodynka Tragedy, anti-Semitic pogroms, Bloody Sunday, the violent suppression of the 1905 Revolution, the execution of political opponents and his perceived responsibility for the Russo-Japanese War, he was given the nickname Nicholas the Bloody by his political adversaries.

p6s3.title: Nicholas II of Russia
p6s3.text: Soviet historiography portrayed Nicholas as a weak and incompetent leader, whose decisions led to military defeats and the deaths of millions of his subjects.

p8s0.title: Russian Revolution
p8s0.text: The Russian Revolution was a pair of revolutions in Russia in 1917 which dismantled the Tsarist autocracy and led to the rise of the Soviet Union.

p8s1.title: Russian Revolution
p8s1.text: The Russian Empire collapsed with the abdication of Emperor Nicholas II and the old regime was replaced by a provisional government during the first revolution of February 1917 (March in the Gregorian calendar; the older Julian calendar was in use in Russia at the time).

p8s2.title: Russian Revolution
p8s2.text: Alongside it arose grassroots community assemblies (called 'soviets') which contended for authority.

p8s3.title: Russian Revolution
p8s3.text: In the second revolution that October, the Provisional Government was toppled and all power was given to the soviets.

p2s0.title: Charles Sydney Gibbes
p2s0.text: Charles Sydney Gibbes (19 January 1876 – 24 March 1963) was a British academic who from 1908 to 1917 served as the English tutor to the children of Emperor Nicholas II of Russia.

p2s1.title: Charles Sydney Gibbes
p2s1.text: When Nicholas abdicated the throne in March 1917 Gibbes voluntarily accompanied the Imperial family into exile to the Siberian village of Tobolsk.

p2s2.title: Charles Sydney Gibbes
p2s2.text: After the family was murdered in 1918 Gibbes returned to the United Kingdom and eventually became an Orthodox monk, adopting the name of "Nicholas" in commemoration of Nicholas II.

p2s3.title: Charles Sydney Gibbes
p2s3.text: He died in 1963, and is buried at Headington cemetery, Oxford, Oxfordshire, England.

p0s0.title: Grand Duke Vladimir Alexandrovich of Russia
p0s0.text: Grand Duke Vladimir Alexandrovich of Russia ("Влади́мир Александрович") ) (22 April 1847 – 17 February 1909) was a son of Emperor Alexander II of Russia, a brother of Emperor Alexander III of Russia and the senior Grand Duke of the House of Romanov during the reign of his nephew, Emperor Nicholas II.

p3s0.title: October Manifesto
p3s0.text: The October Manifesto (Russian: Октябрьский манифест, Манифест 17 октября ), officially The Manifesto on the Improvement of the State Order (Манифест об усовершенствовании государственного порядка), is a document that served as a precursor to the Russian Empire's first constitution, which would be adopted the next year.

p3s1.title: October Manifesto
p3s1.text: The Manifesto was issued by Emperor Nicholas II, under the influence of Sergei Witte, on 30 October [O.S. 17 October] 1905 as a response to the Russian Revolution of 1905.

p3s2.title: October Manifesto
p3s2.text: Nicholas strenuously resisted these ideas, but gave in after his first choice to head a military dictatorship, Grand Duke Nicholas, threatened to shoot himself in the head if the Tsar did not accept Witte's suggestion.

p3s3.title: October Manifesto
p3s3.text: Nicholas reluctantly agreed, and issued what became known as the October Manifesto, promising basic civil rights and an elected parliament called the Duma, without whose approval no laws were to be enacted in Russia in the future.

p3s4.title: October Manifesto
p3s4.text: According to his memoirs Witte did not force the Tsar to sign the October Manifesto, which was proclaimed in all the churches.

p1s0.title: Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich of Russia
p1s0.text: Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich of Russia ("Сергей Александрович"; May 11, 1857 – February 17, 1905) was the fifth son and seventh child of Emperor Alexander II of Russia.

p1s1.title: Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich of Russia
p1s1.text: He was an influential figure during the reigns of his brother Emperor Alexander III of Russia and his nephew Emperor Nicholas II, who was also his brother in law through Sergei's marriage to Elizabeth the sister of Tsarina Alexandra.

p9s0.title: Grand Duke Alexander Alexandrovich of Russia
p9s0.text: Grand Duke Alexander Alexandrovich of Russia (Russian: Великий Князь Александр Александрович Романов; 7 June 1869 – 2 May 1870) was the infant son of Emperor Alexander III–the heir apparent, styled "Tsesarevich", to the Russian throne as the eldest living son of Emperor Alexander II–and his consort, Marie Fyodorovna of Russia.

p9s1.title: Grand Duke Alexander Alexandrovich of Russia
p9s1.text: He was Alexander and Marie's second child, second son, and the younger brother of the future Emperor Nicholas II.

p9s2.title: Grand Duke Alexander Alexandrovich of Russia
p9s2.text: He died of meningitis in 1870, one month before his first birthday.

p9s3.title: Grand Duke Alexander Alexandrovich of Russia
p9s3.text: "The doctors maintain he did not suffer, but we suffered terribly to see and hear him," his mother wrote to her own mother, Queen Louise of Denmark.
